questions.question: A user runs `python -m httpie` and presses Ctrl+C while the command is still starting up. What does the package's entry-point `main()` in `__main__.py` do in that case?
questions.answer: It catches the KeyboardInterrupt and returns the numeric value of the Ctrl+C exit status, which is passed to sys.exit
distractors: It lets the KeyboardInterrupt propagate so Python prints a traceback and exits
It retries importing and calling the core main function once before giving up
It returns a generic success status because no request was sent yet
choices: It lets the KeyboardInterrupt propagate so Python prints a traceback and exits
It catches the KeyboardInterrupt and returns the numeric value of the Ctrl+C exit status, which is passed to sys.exit
It retries importing and calling the core main function once before giving up
It returns a generic success status because no request was sent yet
questions.explanation: The import of `httpie.core.main` and the call to it sit inside a try block. A KeyboardInterrupt there is caught, mapped to `ExitStatus.ERROR_CTRL_C`, and its `.value` is returned to `sys.exit` (`httpie/__main__.py:7-14`, `httpie/__main__.py:19`). Because the handler catches the interrupt, no traceback is printed, and nothing is retried or reported as success.

questions.question: Why does `compat.py` wrap `from functools import cached_property` in a try/except and define its own `cached_property` class in the except branch?
questions.answer: So the code still works on Python versions whose functools has no cached_property, by providing an equivalent decorator
distractors: To replace the standard library version with a faster one on every Python version
To add thread locking around property access that functools does not provide
To make cached values expire after a configurable timeout
choices: To replace the standard library version with a faster one on every Python version
So the code still works on Python versions whose functools has no cached_property, by providing an equivalent decorator
To make cached values expire after a configurable timeout
To add thread locking around property access that functools does not provide
questions.explanation: The local class is only defined when the import raises ImportError. The comment says it can be removed once Python versions below 3.8 are no longer supported (`httpie/compat.py:20-25`). On newer Pythons the standard library version is used, so the shim is not a speed-up. Its `__get__` simply stores the result in `instance.__dict__` (`httpie/compat.py:58-67`), with no locking and no expiry.

questions.question: A user puts some options under `default_options` in their HTTPie `config.json`. How do these options reach the argument parser on a normal `http` run?
questions.answer: raw_main puts the configured default options in front of the command-line arguments before parsing, so options typed on the command line come later in the list
distractors: raw_main adds the configured options after the command-line arguments, so the config file always overrides the command line
The Config object passes them to the parser separately, after it has finished parsing the command line
They are applied only by program() after a request has been built, so they never go through the parser
choices: The Config object passes them to the parser separately, after it has finished parsing the command line
They are applied only by program() after a request has been built, so they never go through the parser
raw_main puts the configured default options in front of the command-line arguments before parsing, so options typed on the command line come later in the list
raw_main adds the configured options after the command-line arguments, so the config file always overrides the command line
questions.explanation: `Config` starts with `default_options: []` and exposes it as a property (`httpie/config.py:139-150`). `raw_main` reads `env.config.default_options` and builds `args = env.config.default_options + args` before calling `parser.parse_args` (`httpie/core.py:48-49`, `httpie/core.py:77-80`). So the defaults come first, not last, and they go through the same parser. This also only happens when `use_default_options` is true.

questions.question: While `program()` is sending a request, the `requests` library raises a Timeout. How does that end up as the process exit code?
questions.answer: raw_main catches the Timeout around main_program, logs a timeout message, and returns ExitStatus.ERROR_TIMEOUT; the entry-point main returns its value to sys.exit
distractors: program() catches the Timeout itself and returns ERROR_TIMEOUT before raw_main sees it
The Timeout propagates to __main__.main, which catches all exceptions and turns them into the Ctrl+C status
raw_main's generic Exception handler logs it and returns the plain ERROR status
choices: program() catches the Timeout itself and returns ERROR_TIMEOUT before raw_main sees it
The Timeout propagates to __main__.main, which catches all exceptions and turns them into the Ctrl+C status
raw_main's generic Exception handler logs it and returns the plain ERROR status
raw_main catches the Timeout around main_program, logs a timeout message, and returns ExitStatus.ERROR_TIMEOUT; the entry-point main returns its value to sys.exit
questions.explanation: `program()` is documented as "the main program without error handling" (`httpie/core.py:170-174`). In `raw_main`, the call to `main_program` has a dedicated `except requests.Timeout` that sets `ExitStatus.ERROR_TIMEOUT` and logs the timeout (`httpie/core.py:99-117`). That handler comes before the generic `Exception` handler, so the generic one never sees a Timeout. `__main__.main` only catches KeyboardInterrupt and returns `exit_status.value` (`httpie/__main__.py:7-14`).

questions.concept: Separating error handling from program logic
questions.question: `raw_main` takes the parser and the program to run as parameters (`parser`, `main_program`), and `main()` passes in the HTTP parser and `program`. What does this design make possible?
questions.answer: Another command can reuse the same argument decoding, plugin loading, default-option handling and exception-to-exit-status mapping by passing its own parser and program
distractors: It lets program() run several requests in parallel threads, each with its own parser
It is needed for argparse to work at all, because argparse needs the program function at construction time
It moves error handling into program() so each command can format its own tracebacks
choices: Another command can reuse the same argument decoding, plugin loading, default-option handling and exception-to-exit-status mapping by passing its own parser and program
It is needed for argparse to work at all, because argparse needs the program function at construction time
It lets program() run several requests in parallel threads, each with its own parser
It moves error handling into program() so each command can format its own tracebacks
questions.explanation: `raw_main` handles daemon mode, plugin loading, default options, `--debug`/`--traceback`, and maps exceptions to `ExitStatus`. It then calls whichever `main_program` it was given (`httpie/core.py:32-143`). `main()` is a thin wrapper that supplies the HTTP parser and `program` (`httpie/core.py:146-167`), so the same wrapper can run a different parser and program. Error handling stays in `raw_main`, not in `program` (`httpie/core.py:170-174`). The code has no threading, and argparse does not depend on this.

questions.question: `compat.py` sets `cookiejar.DefaultCookiePolicy = HTTPieCookiePolicy` at import time instead of attaching the policy to one cookie jar. If that line were removed, what behavior would most likely be lost?
questions.answer: Cookies marked Secure would no longer be treated as sendable to plain-HTTP localhost hosts, because the custom localhost check would not be in effect
distractors: All cookies would stop being sent, because the standard cookiejar has no default policy without this line
Secure cookies would start leaking to every plain-HTTP host, because the standard policy ignores the Secure flag
Session files could no longer be loaded, because the session code reads the policy class to parse JSON
choices: All cookies would stop being sent, because the standard cookiejar has no default policy without this line
Cookies marked Secure would no longer be treated as sendable to plain-HTTP localhost hosts, because the custom localhost check would not be in effect
Session files could no longer be loaded, because the session code reads the policy class to parse JSON
Secure cookies would start leaking to every plain-HTTP host, because the standard policy ignores the Secure flag
questions.explanation: `HTTPieCookiePolicy.return_ok_secure` first defers to the standard check and then also accepts `localhost` and `*.localhost` hosts (`httpie/cookies.py:9-25`). The comment in compat explains why the class is installed globally: the request does not carry the policy attached to the jar, so the global default is changed instead (`httpie/compat.py:9-12`). Without the patch, the standard policy, which only accepts secure protocols, is used again. Cookies would not stop entirely, and secure cookies would not leak to every host.

questions.answer: core.program maps the status with http_status_to_exit_status to an ExitStatus, raw_main returns it, and __main__.main passes its integer value to sys.exit
distractors: __main__.main inspects the HTTP response itself and picks an exit code from the status line
A 404 raises an exception in core.program that __main__.main catches and converts to an exit code
The exit code stays success because only network errors and timeouts change the exit status
choices: The exit code stays success because only network errors and timeouts change the exit status
A 404 raises an exception in core.program that __main__.main catches and converts to an exit code
__main__.main inspects the HTTP response itself and picks an exit code from the status line
core.program maps the status with http_status_to_exit_status to an ExitStatus, raw_main returns it, and __main__.main passes its integer value to sys.exit
questions.explanation: With args.check_status, program() calls http_status_to_exit_status, which returns ERROR_HTTP_4XX for 4xx codes (httpie/core.py:230-231, httpie/status.py:33-35); raw_main returns that value and __main__.main returns exit_status.value to sys.exit (httpie/__main__.py:9-19). __main__ never sees the response, and no exception is raised for a 404.

questions.question: Why does daemons._start_process add httpie.__main__.__file__ to the command when HTTPie is not frozen?
questions.answer: In that case sys.executable is the Python interpreter, so it needs the path of the entry-point script to run HTTPie in the new process
distractors: It makes the child process import httpie.__main__ to share the parent's in-memory state
sys.executable is the http binary, and the file path is passed as the URL argument
It is required on every platform so the child can find the installed plugins directory
choices: sys.executable is the http binary, and the file path is passed as the URL argument
It is required on every platform so the child can find the installed plugins directory
In that case sys.executable is the Python interpreter, so it needs the path of the entry-point script to run HTTPie in the new process
It makes the child process import httpie.__main__ to share the parent's in-memory state
questions.explanation: The comment says that when not frozen sys.executable points to the Python interpreter, so the code appends the __main__ file path to make `python <path> task --daemon` (httpie/internal/daemons.py:22-29); that script then calls httpie.core.main via its __name__ == '__main__' block (httpie/__main__.py:17-19). A new process shares no memory with the parent, and a frozen build skips the path because sys.executable is already the http binary.

questions.answer: False

choices: True

questions.answer: Add a member to the ExitStatus enum and return it from the matching exception handler in core.raw_main; __main__.main needs no change
distractors: Add a new except clause to __main__.main that catches the error and returns a hard-coded integer
Change __main__.main to translate each ExitStatus into an integer with its own lookup table
Raise SystemExit with the new code from the request code so it bypasses ExitStatus entirely

Change __main__.main to translate each ExitStatus into an integer with its own lookup table

questions.question: On Linux, _spawn_posix forks twice and calls os.setsid() in between. What is this sequence meant to achieve for the user who just ran an `http` command?
questions.answer: The background task becomes detached from the user's process, so their command can finish without waiting for the task
distractors: The task runs twice in parallel so one copy can retry if the other fails
The task inherits the user's terminal so it can print its result when it finishes
The parent process waits for both children to exit before returning an exit status
choices: The task runs twice in parallel so one copy can retry if the other fails
The background task becomes detached from the user's process, so their command can finish without waiting for the task
The task inherits the user's terminal so it can print its result when it finishes
The parent process waits for both children to exit before returning an exit status
questions.explanation: The docstring says the double fork detaches from the parent "so that we don't block the user" (httpie/internal/daemons.py:56-59); the original process returns right after the first fork (daemons.py:67-69) and the intermediate child exits after the second (daemons.py:76-78). The task does not keep the terminal: stdin/stdout/stderr are closed (daemons.py:83-85), and nothing waits for the children in the parent.

questions.question: After the double fork on macOS (Darwin), the code starts a subprocess and then calls process.communicate() to wait for it. Why is waiting acceptable here even though the whole point is not to block the user?
questions.answer: The waiting happens in the already-detached grandchild, so only the background process blocks, not the user's command
distractors: communicate() returns immediately on macOS because stdout and stderr are discarded
macOS cannot run the task without a parent attached, so the user's process must wait anyway
Waiting lets the subprocess send its output back to the user's terminal
choices: The waiting happens in the already-detached grandchild, so only the background process blocks, not the user's command
Waiting lets the subprocess send its output back to the user's terminal
communicate() returns immediately on macOS because stdout and stderr are discarded
macOS cannot run the task without a parent attached, so the user's process must wait anyway
questions.explanation: The comment notes double-fork alone is not reliable on macOS, so a subprocess isolates the task, and "since we already completed the fork procedure we can simply join the process" (httpie/internal/daemons.py:87-93). By then the user's original process has already returned from the first fork (daemons.py:67-69). The output is not sent back: _start_process redirects it to DEVNULL (daemons.py:29).

questions.answer: spawn_daemon appends '--daemon' to the arguments, and raw_main checks is_daemon_mode(args) first and hands off to run_daemon_task before plugins load or arguments are parsed
distractors: spawn_daemon sets a PYTHONPATH environment variable that core.main reads to choose daemon mode
httpie/__main__.py inspects the task name and calls the task function directly without going through core.main
The argument parser recognises 'fetch_updates' as a subcommand and routes it to the update checker
choices: The argument parser recognises 'fetch_updates' as a subcommand and routes it to the update checker
httpie/__main__.py inspects the task name and calls the task function directly without going through core.main
spawn_daemon appends '--daemon' to the arguments, and raw_main checks is_daemon_mode(args) first and hands off to run_daemon_task before plugins load or arguments are parsed
spawn_daemon sets a PYTHONPATH environment variable that core.main reads to choose daemon mode
questions.explanation: spawn_daemon builds args as [task, '--daemon'] (httpie/internal/daemons.py:113), and the child runs either httpie/__main__.py via _start_process (daemons.py:26-29) or core.main(['http'] + args) directly (daemons.py:97). In httpie/core.py:43-44, raw_main returns run_daemon_task(env, args) when is_daemon_mode(args), before plugin loading (core.py:46) and parser.parse_args (core.py:77). PYTHONPATH (daemons.py:117) only makes the package importable; it does not select the mode.

questions.question: _start_process adds httpie/__main__.py to the command only when is_frozen is false, and spawn_daemon sets PYTHONPATH only in that case too. What problem would appear if HTTPie were packaged as a frozen binary and the code still added the __main__.py path?
questions.answer: sys.executable is already the http binary, so the script path would be passed to HTTPie as an extra command-line argument rather than run as a Python script
distractors: The frozen binary would start a second Python interpreter and run the task twice
is_windows would be evaluated incorrectly, so the POSIX branch would run on Windows
The child would inherit an empty environment because os.environ.copy() fails in frozen builds
choices: The child would inherit an empty environment because os.environ.copy() fails in frozen builds
The frozen binary would start a second Python interpreter and run the task twice
is_windows would be evaluated incorrectly, so the POSIX branch would run on Windows
sys.executable is already the http binary, so the script path would be passed to HTTPie as an extra command-line argument rather than run as a Python script
questions.explanation: The comment in httpie/internal/daemons.py:24-25 says a frozen sys.executable "points to the binary (http)", while otherwise it is the Python interpreter that needs __main__.py as its script (daemons.py:26-28). is_frozen comes from getattr(sys, 'frozen', False) in httpie/compat.py:15, and httpie/__main__.py:1 documents it as the entry point used as `python -m httpie`. is_windows is a separate check (compat.py:14) that this branch does not affect.

Running inline would make the update warning appear twice because check_updates is decorated with _update_checker

choices: _fetch_updates makes a blocking HTTP request to the package index, and doing that inline would delay or break every user command that triggers a fetch; a detached daemon keeps the user's request path fast
The version file can only be written while holding a lock, and only a separate process is allowed to take that lock
Running inline would make the update warning appear twice because check_updates is decorated with _update_checker
The daemon runs with elevated privileges so it can write the version file into a protected directory
questions.explanation: In httpie/core.py:97-100, check_updates(env) is called right before main_program, and the _update_checker wrapper then calls maybe_fetch_updates (httpie/internal/update_warnings.py:97-102), which calls fetch_updates with lazy=True, so spawn_daemon('fetch_updates') is used (update_warnings.py:55-57). _fetch_updates performs requests.get on PACKAGE_INDEX_LINK (update_warnings.py:44), and daemons.py:56-59 says detaching exists so the user is not blocked while the release fetcher runs. The lockfile (update_warnings.py:51) is used in the normal process as well, so it is not a reason to need a separate process.

questions.question: In the POSIX grandchild, the task runs inside suppress(BaseException) and the function always ends with os._exit(0). Suppose someone replaced os._exit(0) with a plain return and removed the suppress block. What would be the most serious consequence?
questions.answer: The forked grandchild would return into the copied call stack (check_updates → raw_main) and continue running the user's original command in the background, or let an exception escape into that inherited code
distractors: The parent process would become a zombie because the grandchild would never be reaped
The update warning would be printed on the user's terminal even when disable_update_warnings is set
The version file would be deleted because the lockfile is released without a final write
choices: The forked grandchild would return into the copied call stack (check_updates → raw_main) and continue running the user's original command in the background, or let an exception escape into that inherited code
The parent process would become a zombie because the grandchild would never be reaped
The version file would be deleted because the lockfile is released without a final write
The update warning would be printed on the user's terminal even when disable_update_warnings is set
questions.explanation: A forked child continues from the same point as its parent, and here that point is inside spawn_daemon, which was called from fetch_updates/maybe_fetch_updates in the check_updates wrapper (httpie/internal/update_warnings.py:55-57, 97-102), itself called from raw_main just before main_program (httpie/core.py:98-100). os._exit(0) (httpie/internal/daemons.py:99) ends the grandchild without unwinding that stack, and suppress(BaseException) around main(['http'] + args) (daemons.py:96-97) stops a task failure from leaking into the inherited code. The intermediate child also exits with os._exit (daemons.py:78), and the disable flag is checked separately (update_warnings.py:142), so the distractors do not follow from this change.

questions.answer: The value stored in the instance's __dict__ during the first read is returned, so the wrapped method is not called again.
distractors: The wrapped method runs again, and its new result overwrites the value that was cached on the first read.
The value is looked up in a cache shared by every instance of the class, so all instances get the same result.
A TypeError is raised, because one cached_property cannot be read more than once on the same object.

questions.question: In the ConnectionError handler, raw_main calls unwrap_context before deciding what to report. What would break if it passed the ConnectionError straight to handle_generic_error?

distractors: The request would be retried automatically, because handle_generic_error re-sends requests that failed with a ConnectionError

questions.question: When you run `http` or `python -m httpie`, the entry function wraps the call to the core main in a try block that catches KeyboardInterrupt. What does this achieve?
questions.answer: Pressing Ctrl+C ends the program with a defined exit code for interruption, returned to the shell, instead of a Python traceback.
distractors: Pressing Ctrl+C makes HTTPie retry the current request once before it exits.
Pressing Ctrl+C makes HTTPie save the current session to disk before it exits.
Pressing Ctrl+C is treated as a successful run, so scripts never see a failure.

questions.question: On older Pythons, compat.py supplies its own `cached_property`. What happens the first time code reads an attribute decorated with it on an object, and then reads it again?
questions.answer: The first read calls the method and stores the result in that object's `__dict__`, so later reads return the stored value without calling the method again.
distractors: Every read calls the method again, and the decorator only makes the call look like an attribute.
The first read stores the result on the class, so every instance of that class shares one value.
The first read stores the result in a module-level cache keyed by the method name.

distractors: `raw_main` puts them after the user's own args, so the config file always wins over the command line.

questions.question: compat.py assigns `cookiejar.DefaultCookiePolicy = HTTPieCookiePolicy` when it is imported, instead of passing the policy to a specific cookie jar. What is the trade-off of this design?
questions.answer: It works around requests not carrying a jar's attached policy, so Secure cookies can be sent to localhost over plain HTTP. The cost is a process-wide side effect at import time: any code that creates the default policy gets HTTPie's version.
distractors: It limits the new policy to HTTPie's own Session objects, so the only cost is that third-party code cannot reuse the policy.

concepts.name: From HTTPie command line to printed HTTP exchange
concepts.definition: How an HTTPie terminal command turns into an HTTP request and how the response is formatted and printed. In the grounded code this covers: the `http`/`https` commands (which send requests) versus the `httpie` manager command (which only manages plugins and the CLI); the cookie policy that decides which stored cookies go out with a request; the transport adapter that builds the response object while keeping repeated headers; and the order in which request and response parts (headers, body, separators, metadata) appear in the printed output.

items.caption: Start at the entry you type. `httpie/manager/core.py` belongs to the `httpie` manager command. It only sends `plugins` and `cli` subcommands to tasks (lines 26-42). If you type `httpie` with no subcommand, it stops with a message telling you to send requests with `http`/`https` instead (lines 9-23, 34-35). So a request is built only when you start with `http` or `https`.

questions.question: A frontend developer types just `httpie` in the terminal and presses Enter, hoping to try a request. What does this code do?
questions.answer: It stops with an error that lists the valid subcommands and shows an example using `http POST pie.dev/post hello=world`
distractors: It sends a GET request to a default host and prints the response
It opens an interactive prompt that asks for the method and URL
It prints the installed plugin list and exits successfully
questions.explanation: When `args.action` is None, `program` calls `parser.error(MSG_NAKED_INVOCATION)` (httpie/manager/core.py:34-35). That message combines the list of subcommands with a hint to use `http`/`https` (httpie/manager/core.py:9-23). Nothing here builds a request or opens a prompt.

questions.question: Running `httpie plugins list` turns its arguments into an HTTP request and sends it, just like `http` does.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: For `plugins`, `program` hands off to `dispatch_cli_task`, which looks up a task in `CLI_TASKS` and runs it (httpie/manager/core.py:26-30, 37-38). It builds no request. The help text says this command is only for managing plugins (httpie/manager/core.py:9-11).

items.caption: Before a request goes out, HTTPie decides which stored cookies to attach. `HTTPieCookiePolicy` extends the standard library cookie policy. A cookie marked Secure is normally sent only over a secure protocol. HTTPie also treats `localhost` and any `*.localhost` host as secure, the way Chrome and Firefox do (httpie/cookies.py:9-25). This matters if you test a local dev server over plain http.

questions.question: Your dev server at http://localhost:3000 set a cookie marked Secure. On the next plain-http request to the same server, does this policy allow HTTPie to send that cookie?
questions.answer: Yes, because the policy counts the host `localhost` as a secure location even without https
distractors: No, because Secure cookies are only ever sent over https
Only if the URL uses 127.0.0.1 instead of the name localhost
Only after the cookie is copied into a named session file
questions.explanation: If the parent check fails because the protocol is not secure, `return_ok_secure` falls back to `_is_local_host` (httpie/cookies.py:12-20). That check returns True for the host `localhost` (httpie/cookies.py:25). The code matches host names only, so 127.0.0.1 is not treated this way.

questions.question: Which plain-http host would this policy NOT treat as a secure place to send a Secure cookie?
questions.answer: app.localhost.example.com
distractors: localhost
api.localhost
dev.app.localhost
questions.explanation: `_is_local_host` accepts only the exact name `localhost` or a name that ends with `.localhost` (httpie/cookies.py:4-5, 25). `app.localhost.example.com` ends with `.example.com`, so the check fails. The other three hosts all pass.

questions.question: For an https URL, the policy still runs the localhost name check before deciding whether a Secure cookie may be sent.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: `return_ok_secure` calls the parent check first and returns True right away if the protocol is secure (httpie/cookies.py:12-14). The localhost check on line 20 runs only when that first check fails.

items.caption: When the server replies, the `requests` library builds a response object. HTTPie plugs in its own transport adapter, `HTTPieHTTPAdapter`. It lets `requests` do the normal work, then swaps the headers for an `HTTPHeadersDict`. That keeps every header that appears more than once, such as several Set-Cookie lines, so all of them can be printed (httpie/adapters.py:5-13).

questions.question: A server sends back two separate `Set-Cookie` headers. Why does HTTPie's adapter replace the response headers with an `HTTPHeadersDict`?
questions.answer: So that both headers with the same name are kept instead of being merged into one
distractors: So that header names are sorted alphabetically before colored printing
So that header names are lowercased before the next request is sent
So that hop-by-hop headers are removed from the printed response
questions.explanation: The docstring says the wrapper exists 'to preserve multiple headers that have the same name' (httpie/adapters.py:8-9). Line 12 builds `HTTPHeadersDict` from the raw response headers. The code does no sorting, lowercasing or filtering.

questions.question: HTTPieHTTPAdapter replaces the whole response-building step, so HTTPie's own code builds the status and body instead of the requests library.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: `build_response` first calls `super().build_response(req, resp)`, so `requests` still builds the response (httpie/adapters.py:11). HTTPie then replaces only `response.headers` (httpie/adapters.py:12).

items.caption: This test helper describes the shape of HTTPie's printed output as a sequence of tokens: request headers, response headers, response metadata, body and separator. Compare the raw sequences with the terminal ones. Terminal output adds a separator after each message, and the `_META` variant adds response metadata at the very end (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:4-52).

questions.question: According to `TERMINAL_EXCHANGE`, in what order do the parts appear when HTTPie prints both the request and the response to the terminal?
questions.answer: Request headers, request body, separator, response headers, response body, separator
distractors: Response headers, response body, separator, request headers, request body, separator
Request headers, response headers, separator, request body, response body, separator
Request headers, request body, response headers, response body, with no separators
questions.explanation: `TERMINAL_EXCHANGE` is `TERMINAL_REQUEST` followed by `TERMINAL_RESPONSE` (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:45-48). Each of those is headers, then body, then a separator (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:21-28, 37-44). The request always comes before the response, and the headers and body of one message stay together.

questions.question: What separates the expected raw exchange (`RAW_EXCHANGE`) from the terminal exchange (`TERMINAL_EXCHANGE`)?
questions.answer: Raw output has one separator, between request and response; terminal output ends each message with a separator
distractors: Raw output leaves out the bodies and keeps only headers
Terminal output leaves out the request headers
Raw output always ends with the response metadata
questions.explanation: `RAW_EXCHANGE` puts a single `SEPARATOR` between the request and the response (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:29-33). The terminal versions add a `SEPARATOR` after each message (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:37-48). Both include headers and bodies, and only `TERMINAL_EXCHANGE_META` adds `RESPONSE_META` (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:49-52).

questions.question: In `TERMINAL_EXCHANGE_META`, the response metadata is printed before the response headers.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: `TERMINAL_EXCHANGE_META` is the full `TERMINAL_EXCHANGE` with `Expect.RESPONSE_META` added at the end (tests/utils/matching/tokens.py:49-52). So the metadata comes after the response headers, body and separator.
